1. The animation shows how often US consumer prices (CPI-U) have risen at different yearly rates over past stretches of time. It uses US history only, and a caption says it is not a forecast. The bars sit on a scale labeled "raise a year" on one side and "all stretches" on the other. Each bar appears to show the share of historical stretches in which prices rose at or above a given yearly rate.

2. The bars are added one at a time, and the view changes from a 3D angle to a flat one. First comes 2% with 2.4%. Then 3% with 42.4% is added. Then 3.1% is added, marked "half", and this is the median. Frame 4 adds the note "a median of the past, not an expectation". Frames 5 and 6 add a top bar at 6.38% labeled "all · Carl's stretch", and an "ILLUSTRATIVE" tag appears. Taken together, the higher the yearly rise, the larger the share of stretches it covers.

3. Over past stretches, prices rose by at least 2% a year only a small share of the time (2.4%). They rose by about 3% a year in 42.4% of stretches, and by about 3.1% a year in half of them. To cover every stretch, the rise has to reach 6.38% a year, which is the worst case, "Carl's stretch". In short, a flat payout can lose a lot of buying power in some periods, and the typical rise has been around 3% a year. The "ILLUSTRATIVE" tag means the 6.38% case is an example and not a prediction.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might infer that a payout fixed in dollars loses buying power over time, and that a payout with annual raises might be worth comparing. That inference is mine. The animation only presents the history, and it warns that this is not a forecast.

5. The animation did not suggest the advice in 4. It is my own conclusion. The animation only presents historical figures, with captions saying they are not a forecast or an expectation.
